# Dependencies without lock-in {#sec-dependencies}

A dependency provider is a delivery choice. The code that consumes a library should stay the
same when that choice changes.

## `find_package()` is the boundary {#sec-find-package}

Ask CMake for a package, then link its imported target. vcpkg, a system installation, or a
locally built package can all provide the same target.

::: {.snippet source="CMakeLists.txt"}

```cmake
find_package(cpptrace CONFIG REQUIRED)
find_package(glaze CONFIG REQUIRED) # demo
```

:::

Finding a package makes its imported target available. Sketchbook links the imported
`glaze::glaze` target privately into the sketchbook feature:

::: {.snippet source="src/sketchbook/CMakeLists.txt"}

```cmake
target_link_libraries(app_sketchbook
    PRIVATE Qt::Concurrent glaze::glaze app_controls\n)
```

:::

## Choose the provider for the job {#sec-dependency-families}

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Package manager

Use vcpkg or Conan when a project has several dependencies or targets several platforms.
They resolve versions and cache binaries. Sketchbook uses vcpkg for that repeatability.
The tradeoff is an extra toolchain and an initial build or download. A cache pays off when
many machines or CI jobs use the same dependency versions.

### CMake-native source

Use `FetchContent` for a small, tightly controlled dependency when building it as part of
your project is acceptable. Pin the revision and expect its build to become part of yours.
This keeps the setup in CMake, but a source download becomes part of configuration and each
build needs the dependency's sources and build requirements.

### Vendored source

Use a submodule, subtree, or copied source when you maintain a patch or develop the library
beside the app. You own updates and build time, but gain direct control.
The repository also carries the maintenance burden: review upstream changes, keep patches
current, and make sure the dependency's license remains available.

:::
:::

## Reproducibility is the payoff {#sec-reproducibility}

A lock file, a manifest, and a pinned provider make a build explainable. They do not remove
platform work, but they stop an update on one machine from silently changing everyone else's
build.

## A manifest records the dependency set {#sec-vcpkg}

The template lists its libraries in `vcpkg.json` and pins vcpkg itself as a submodule. The
vcpkg toolchain reads the manifest during CMake configuration. A triplet describes a target
platform and build choices; a binary cache can reuse a dependency build rather than compiling
it on every CI run. A pinned baseline controls versions, but the compiler, platform, flags,
and dependency features also affect the resulting binary.

CI uses an installed Qt for its normal build. To build Qt through vcpkg for a configured
build directory, select it before running the workflow:

```sh
cmake --preset dev -DAPP_USE_VCPKG_QT=ON
cmake --workflow --preset dev
```

The option is stored per build directory. Building Qt can take substantially longer than
using an installed kit; the cache is especially useful for repeated release builds.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Detail: Qt is a dependency too

For everyday development, use the installed Qt kit selected by `Qt6_ROOT`. Building Qt
through vcpkg gives a controlled, reproducible release environment, at the cost of a much
slower first configure. Both routes end at the same `find_package(Qt6 ...)` boundary.
:::

::: {.more}
**Template:** `vcpkg.json`, `external/vcpkg/`, and `CMakeLists.txt`

**Read more:** [vcpkg manifest mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/vcpkg/concepts/manifest-mode).
:::
